extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, communications professionals, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on planning and executing public-relations campaigns: how to reach and influence publics through existing media, audience analysis, timing, and appeals to human psychology. Emphasizes practical limits and techniques for projecting a client's point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion cannot be manufactured
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is not responsible for public opinion; he cannot manufacture sympathy from thin air. He can intensify or dissipate existing sympathy but cannot create it where none exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Margaret Sanger evokes enthusiasm with sympathetic audiences but risks abuse with hostile groups; Madam Curie succeeded because public sentiment had been prepared. Use efforts to work where receptive elements already exist rather than to invent public sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations to PR effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: There are always limitations to the effectiveness of public relations; the counsel cannot force people to standardize their points of view or to persist in established beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established points of view persist because they satisfy real or assumed human needs. Counsel must be realistic about what can be changed and focus on achievable modifications rather than wholesale attitude manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach the public only through established mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication; it is not feasible to build up independent organs for broad influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing channels include the daily press, magazines, lecture circuits, advertising media, motion pictures, radio, etc. Counsel should plan campaigns assuming use of these established media rather than creating new mass channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the media forms people are accustomed to
rubrics_metrics.description: People accept facts which come to them through existing channels and like to hear new things in accustomed ways; newspapers and other media must provide fresh content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame messages to fit the conventions and expectations of the chosen medium (e.g., newsworthiness for newspapers). Present information in familiar forms so audiences will receive it without needing to seek out unfamiliar sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: First choose form of action, then select media
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert must advise first upon the form of action desirable for the client and secondly must utilize the established mediums of communication to present the point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine strategy and objectives (what action to take) before deciding which media mix will best project that action to relevant publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide appeals and use a wide variety of avenues
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must always sub-divide the appeal of his subject and present it through the widest possible variety of avenues to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and tailor different channels/messages to each segment. Example: railroads used posters for a broad safety appeal; campaigns must use multiple avenues rather than a single broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit interlapping group formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consists of many overlapping groups; individuals belong to multiple groups whose interests interlap, and counsel can utilize these overlaps to reach people through several affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design appeals that hit different group identities of the same individual (e.g., art lover, music lover, sportsman). Examples: Diaghileff Russian Ballet and the Metropolitan Opera House audiences reached through overlapping group appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment publics by specific shared interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the target public into component groups (e.g., dentists, bankers, theatrical owners) and appeal to the strongest interest of each group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted messaging tailored to each subgroup's primary motivations; example: Federation for the Support of Jewish Charities organized appeals to business-interest groups to raise funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the greatest common factor for unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity across heterogeneous groups is usually attainable only by finding the greatest common factor or divisor of all groups to produce broad agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select broad, fundamental appeals (e.g., loyalty, fairness, patriotism) to secure wide acceptance. Examples: wartime campaigns appealed to patriotism and voluntary rationing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit continuous shifting of groups and changing conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The shifting memberships of groups and changing external conditions create opportunities for modifying public opinion; counsel should exploit these shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor social and technological changes (radio, automobile, airplane, economic inflation, strikes) and time messages to leverage increased receptivity produced by these changes (e.g., savings-bank thrift campaigns during inflation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to create new mass channels (cost and feasibility constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovators and innovations cannot realistically create their own channels of communication — building new newspapers, radio stations, or motion-picture distribution is often impractical and disproportionately expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh economic and logistical costs before attempting new channels; examples show newspaper startups and maintaining broad distribution are financially prohibitive for most clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use education/information to build common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: One effective method of creating cohesion is education by information — presenting analyzed facts to increase shared knowledge and self-consciousness of national circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the method public relations counsel primarily avails himself of (vs. patronage or force). Example: Committee on Public Information (George Creel) used multiple modern communication methods to inform and unify public understanding during wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match timing and message to public receptivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Message success depends on public readiness; an idea presented at the wrong time or to an unreceptive group will fail or provoke hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pushing reform topics when public mood is adverse (e.g., prison reform during a crime wave). Seek audiences or subgroups already predisposed or conditions that increase receptivity before launching sensitive appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders both shape and follow public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders (preachers, statesmen, orators) are attentive to public sentiment; they can intensify or dissipate sympathy but often cannot create it independently of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use leaders to amplify campaigns, but recognize their influence depends on preexisting public currents. Example: Admiral Dewey lost public affection despite earlier leadership when actions conflicted with public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome individual and group 'censorship' (psychological barriers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The average citizen acts as an efficient censor via 'logic-proof compartments' and absolutism; these internal barriers keep people from seeing facts in terms of experience and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel must view problems impartially, step outside his own group, and craft messages that penetrate these mental barriers — propaganda, in this sense, is a directed effort to overcome such censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to universal human instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful appeals often invoke universal instincts such as self-preservation (shelter), hunger (food), and sex, which modern commerce and PR harness to influence behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, instinctive imagery and slogans tied to these instincts (examples: cozy home radiator ads, Gulden Mustard food imagery, Woodbury's 'the skin you love to touch', 'Have you had your iron to-day?'). Ensure such appeals are ethically appropriate for the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure content has news value (freshness) for press channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and the press require items that are fresh; news must be presented as timely and of interest to readers across local, state, and international spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Package client information to emphasize timeliness and novelty to satisfy press standards. Avoid relying on media that prioritize freshness unless the campaign can supply genuinely newsworthy material.
